name: Episodic Memory
question: Has the agent been here before?
summary: Records of specific past experiences, such as a run, its steps, outcome and time, retrieved when a similar situation arises. Retrieval scores each episode on recency, importance and relevance. Reflection condenses related episodes into short lessons, such as “PAN lookup timed out last time; retry once, then escalate”.
useCases: Agents that repeat the same mistakes across runs
Operations and support work where past incidents predict fixes
Few-shot examples chosen from the agent’s own successful runs

steps.title: Log episodes
steps.text: Each run becomes a record: task, steps, outcome, time and cost. A PAN lookup that timed out three weeks ago is one episode among thousands.

steps.title: Score importance
steps.text: When writing, an LLM rates importance from 1 to 10. A failed lookup that kept a customer waiting scores 8; “customer said thanks” scores 1.

steps.title: Retrieve by three scores
steps.text: Recency decays by 0.995 per hour, importance comes from the rating, relevance from embedding similarity. Each is min-max normalized, then added.

steps.title: Reflect past a threshold
steps.text: When the importance of new episodes adds up to 150, the agent writes short lessons that cite the episodes they came from.

steps.title: Inject lessons, not transcripts
steps.text: The prompt gets “PAN API times out at month-end; retry once, then escalate”, 40 tokens, instead of five past transcripts.

steps.title: Measure repeat errors
steps.text: Track how often the agent repeats a mistake it has seen before. That rate, not recall, shows whether episodic memory works.

pros: Reflection turns many runs into short, reusable lessons
Retrieval scores are simple and explainable
cons: Weights need tuning: recency can drown relevance
Importance ratings cost an LLM call per episode
Lessons can overgeneralize from a few cases
Logs grow quickly without retention rules
avoidWhen: Tasks with no repetition across runs
Failures that are about facts or state rather than experience

playgroundGuide.scenario: A KYC operations agent is about to run a month-end PAN lookup batch. Its log holds 12 past episodes. Three weeks ago an identical batch failed because the PAN API timed out at month-end; that is the one episode worth reading. Recent episodes are mostly trivial: thanks, balance enquiries, password resets.
controls: Set the weight of recency, importance and relevance, each from 0 to 3.
Choose how many top-ranked episodes reach the prompt.
Turn on reflection to inject short lessons instead of full transcripts.

outputs.name: Ranking
outputs.meaning: The top 6 episodes with normalized recency, importance and relevance, and the weighted score. Highlighted rows reach the prompt.

outputs.name: Relevant failure retrieved
outputs.meaning: Whether the PAN timeout is in the top k, and its rank.

outputs.name: Repeat-error rate
outputs.meaning: Illustrative: 40% if the lesson is missed, 12% with transcripts, 5% with a lesson.

presets.name: Recency-heavy
presets.expect: Weights 3, 1, 1: “Balance enquiry answered” ranks first and the PAN timeout ranks 10 of 12, so it is missed. 1,050 prompt tokens.

presets.name: Equal weights
presets.expect: Weights 1, 1, 1: the PAN timeout ranks first with 2.00 of a possible 3, and trivial episodes drop out.

presets.name: Relevance only
presets.expect: Only similarity counts: the timeout still ranks first, but “PAN verified on first try” comes second despite teaching little.

presets.name: Importance only
presets.expect: The timeout ranks first; the next three are important but unrelated failures, such as the UPI mandate outage.

missions.text: Get the three-week-old PAN timeout into the top 3.
missions.hint: Recency at 3 lets hours-old trivia win. Lower it, or raise relevance.

missions.text: With reflection on, halve the prompt tokens of the start and keep the failure retrieved.
missions.hint: The start costs 1,050 tokens. Lessons cost 60 each.

missions.text: Stop a trivial recent episode from ranking first.
missions.hint: Trivial episodes have importance 1–2 and low relevance; only recency lifts them.

practice.scenario: An IT-operations agent at a payments company logs every incident run: symptoms, steps, outcome, time and importance. When a new alert arrives, it scores past episodes on recency, importance and relevance, min-max normalized, and retrieves the top two with their post-incident lessons, such as “UPI switch timeouts at 23:55 were a certificate expiry; check certs before restarting pods”.

industries.use: Retrieve the most similar past outages before proposing a fix
Recall how the same customer’s last complaint was resolved
Reuse the lesson from the last failed build of the same service

practice.analogy: A pilot’s logbook plus the airline’s incident bulletins. Pilots do not reread every flight; they read the few similar incidents and the lesson each one taught.

library.name: Plain Python + embeddings
library.what: Episodic retrieval is a small scoring function over your episode log; any embedding model and vector store will do.

practice.note: Write a short lesson per episode (or per reflection over several episodes) and inject lessons, not transcripts.

numericDrill.question: Recency decays by 0.995 per hour. What is the recency of an episode that is 100 hours old? Give it to two decimals.

interview.question: How does an agent choose which past episodes to recall?
interview.answer: Score each episode on recency (exponential decay), importance (rated when written) and relevance (similarity to the current situation), normalize each score, weight and add them, and take the top few.

interview.question: What does reflection add to episodic memory?
interview.answer: It condenses many related episodes into a short, cited lesson, so the agent injects one line of guidance instead of several transcripts, saving tokens and generalizing better.

mistakes.mistake: Adding raw scores on different scales
mistakes.fix: Min-max normalize each component before weighting
Inject short lessons that cite their source episodes

quiz.question: Recency decays by 0.995 per hour. What is the recency of an episode 100 hours old, to two decimals?
An episode score adds raw recency (0–1), importance (1–10) and relevance (0–1). What goes wrong?
options: Importance swamps the other two, so any important episode wins
quiz.explanation: Different scales must be normalized before weighting.

quiz.question: Which scores does the Generative Agents retrieval function combine? Select all that apply.
quiz.explanation: Recency, importance and relevance, each normalized, are combined.

quiz.question: An incident agent keeps retrieving “user said thanks” from an hour ago instead of a similar outage from last month. Which weight is too high?
quiz.explanation: A recency weight that is too high lets trivial recent events win.

quiz.question: In Generative Agents, reflection fires when the summed importance of recent events passes what threshold?
quiz.explanation: The paper uses a threshold of 150, which produced about 2–3 reflections a day.

quiz.question: Reflexion reported what pass@1 on HumanEval, compared with 80% for GPT-4?
quiz.explanation: Reflexion reported 91% pass@1 versus 80% for GPT-4.

quiz.question: Which belong in an episode record for a payment-failure agent? Select all that apply.
quiz.explanation: Task, steps, outcome, time and cost describe an episode; card numbers must never be stored.

quiz.question: Min-max normalizing importance scores of 2, 5 and 8 gives what for the score 5?
Five transcripts cost 350 tokens each; one reflected lesson costs 40 tokens. How many tokens does the lesson save?
What is the best success metric for an incident agent’s episodic memory?
quiz.explanation: Whether the agent stops repeating known mistakes is what matters.

quiz.question: A reflection says “Customs API fails on Fridays; switch to manual filing.” Which safeguards are sensible? Select all that apply.
options: Cite the episodes the lesson came from
Review or retire the lesson when new evidence contradicts it
Inject it into every prompt forever, regardless of task
quiz.explanation: Cited, reviewable lessons can be checked; permanent injection and deleting evidence make errors stick.

quiz.question: Episode A is 504 hours old; episode B is 1 hour old. What is A’s recency at 0.995 per hour, to two decimals?
With equal weights on normalized scores, an old failure has recency 0, importance 1 and relevance 1. A trivial recent chat has 1, 0 and 0. Which ranks higher?
How does LangGraph describe episodic memory in agents?
options: Past experiences, often used as few-shot examples
quiz.explanation: LangGraph frames episodic memory as past experiences, often used as examples.

quiz.question: A triage agent’s episodic memory keeps ranking unrelated high-importance episodes first. Which changes help? Select all that apply.
quiz.explanation: Rebalancing toward relevance fixes it; dropping normalization or relevance makes it worse.

quiz.question: When is episodic memory the wrong fix?
options: The agent repeats last week’s deployment mistake
Failures are about a user’s outdated profile facts
Past incidents predict the right fix
quiz.explanation: Stale user facts are a semantic-memory problem.

quiz.question: Top-k is 3 and the relevant failure ranks 10 of 12. After rebalancing it ranks 1. How many prompt tokens does top-k 3 cost at 350 per transcript?
Importance is rated when an episode is written. Who usually rates it?
options: An LLM prompt returning a score from 1 to 10
quiz.explanation: Generative Agents ask the model to rate importance on a 1–10 scale.

quiz.question: Which statements about reflection are correct? Select all that apply.
options: It condenses episodes into higher-level lessons
It removes the need to log episodes
quiz.explanation: Reflection condenses and saves tokens, but lessons can be wrong and still need their source episodes.

quiz.question: Scores normalized: recency 0.2, importance 0.9, relevance 0.8. Weights 1, 1, 2. What is the total?
